newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Witness says he saw thousands killed in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Witness says he saw thousands killed in Rwanda.

text.p: A prosecution witness said on Friday a Hutu militia leader on trial for genocide ordered militiamen in 1994 to surround thousands of people who were then massacred.

The witness, known as Witness A to protect his identity, told a U.N. tribunal Georges Rutaganda told Interahamwe Hutu militiamen to surround a crowd of Tutsi men, women and children one day in April 1994.

"Rutaganda told his Interahamwe to surround the crowd. They had machetes, clubs and guns," said the witness, adding Hutus were asked to show their identity cards and were then allowed to leave the area.
He said the militiamen were joined near the crowd of Tutsis by Rwandan Hutu troops, who brought a sack of hand grenades.
"One soldier launched the hand grenades by throwing them towards the crowd and immediately after that the soldiers and Interahamwe opened fire on the crowd, killing most people," he said.
He said thousands died including his wife and four of his children on the route to the town of Nyanza near the Rwandan capital Kigali. He showed the court a bullet wound in his arm.
He said the soldiers left in the evening, promising to come back the next day and finish their killing. He said Tutsi women including the wounded were raped by soldiers and then killed.
"Soldiers undressed the dead women, saying that the nakedness of a Tutsi woman must be exposed," the witness said.
He said the Tutsis had first taken refuge at a technical school and then decided to head for U.N. headquarters in Kigali but soldiers intercepted them and ordered them towards Nyanza.

The prosecution plans to call a total of 35 witnesses in its case against Rutaganda, who is being tried at the U.N. tribunal in the northern Tanzanian town Arusha. The trial was adjourned until Monday.
The defence team has said that it will try to establish whether in fact a genocide took place or whether the Hutu majority was only trying to defend itself against Tutsi rebels.
Rutaganda, 39, was a vice-president of the Hutu Interahamwe militia, which was held responsible for massacres during the genocide of about 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically-moderate Hutus.

Among other things, Rutaganda is accused of arming Hutu extremists in April 1994 and ordering the murder of Tutsi civilians with machetes, guns, grenades and drowning. The prosecution says some victims were made to dig their own graves.
Rutaganda, a former agricultural engineer and businessman, was charged last May with eight counts of genocide along with other crimes against humanity and has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
Rutaganda's trial, which started on Tuesday, is the second to open at the tribunal in Arusha. The trial of Jean Paul Akayesu which began on January 9 has been suspended until May.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan dismissed two top tribunal officials last month after a U.N. report detailed administrative mismanagement, unqualified staff and legal chaos at Arusha.
